To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
T cells from tumor bearing mice express normal levels and activities of the signal transduction proteins lck, fny, ZAP-7o and CD3-zcta.
T cells from late tumor bearing mice express normal levels (as compared to normal mice) of p56lkc, p59fyc, ZAP-7c, and CD3zeta, despite suppressed cytolytc activity.
tumor-bearing mice do not exhibit loss of lck, p59(fyn), ZAP-70 or CD3-z.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of tumor-induced immune suppression and the role of tumor-derived soluble mediators in this process.
the mechanisms underlying immune suppression in tumor bearing hosts.
the role of the immune system in tumor growth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alterations in the expression of signal transduction molecules in tumor-bearing mice are not responsible for the immune suppression observed during tumor progression.
alterations in TCR signaling molecules are unlikely to be the cause of the profound immune suppression observed in tumor-bearing animals and cancer patients.
the loss of signal transduction molecules is not a general phenomenon in tumor-bearing mice, and that the immune suppression observed is due to other factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tumor-specific suppression is not due to alterations in the levels of lck/fyn/ZAP-70/CD3-zeta.

T cells from tumor bearing mice show normal levels of signal transduction molecules and normal T cell function, until the tumor burden reaches 20% of body weight, when the T cell responses are suppressed.
tumor-specific immune suppression is not due to a lack of signal transduction molecules in the T cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tumor-bearing animals do not exhibit any significant changes in their T cell signal transducers until the tumors have grown to a very large size.
the immune suppression observed in tumor-bearing mice is a consequence of tumor-specific factors, and not of a general defect in T cell function.
tumor-bearing mice can be used as models of cancer patients only for a short period after the initial tumor challenge.
